CUDA graph replay is faster than eager kernel launching primarily because it eliminates the significant CPU overhead associated with managing the GPU. In a traditional eager execution model, the CPU must issue a separate command for every kernel launch, memory copy, and synchronization point. Each of these incurs a fixed cost due to driver validation, state changes, and communication latency over the PCIe bus. By recording a sequence of these operations into a graph, the application captures the entire workflow as a single unit. When the graph is launched, the CPU submits one command rather than hundreds or thousands, drastically reducing the launch latency and allowing the GPU to execute the workload with fewer interruptions.

Furthermore, graphs enable the CUDA runtime and driver to optimize the workload globally. When kernels are launched individually, the runtime must treat each as an isolated event, often inserting conservative barriers or memory flushes to ensure correctness. Because a graph presents the full dependency structure of the application upfront, the driver can see the entire "forest" of operations. This visibility allows it to prune unnecessary synchronization, keep GPU resources (like registers and shared memory) resident across kernel boundaries, and potentially improve scheduling efficiency to keep the compute units busy.
